Stage 4 · Passive and causative together

Three ways of not saying “I did it”

The passive hides the doer. The causative names an arranger. The active says it was you. Choosing between them is most of the skill.

1 · Look at these three sentences about the same street.
Three versions

  • b  The shopkeeper had the lamp posts covered in wool.
  • c  The shopkeeper covered the lamp posts in wool.
  • d  It is believed to have started in the United States.
  • e  She got a knitting group to make the cover.

FormExampleWhat it says

passiveThe post was covered.somebody did; nobody is named

One test settles almost every case: ask who was holding the tools. If it was the subject, use the active. If it was somebody else and the subject paid or asked, use the causative. If nobody in the sentence needs to be responsible, use the passive.

4 · One street, six ways of telling it.
She covered the lamp post.  →  she did it.
The lamp post was covered overnight.  →  nobody named.
It was covered by a local group.  →  the group is the news.
She had the lamp post covered.  →  she arranged it.
She got a group to cover it.  →  she persuaded them.
It is believed to have started in the US.  →  a claim, unattributed.
1 · Read the explanation.
Choosing between the active, the passive and the causative

The three shapes. She covered the post (active: she did it). The post was covered (passive: be + past participle; somebody did it and the sentence does not say who). She had the post covered (causative: have + object + past participle; she arranged it and somebody else did it). The words in the middle of the last two are identical, so the only thing telling them apart is what comes in front.

What each one is for. Use the passive when the doer is unknown, obvious or irrelevant, or when the thing is the topic of the paragraph. Use the causative when the arranging is the point: it puts the client back in the subject position without pretending they did the work. Use the active when somebody is responsible and you are willing to say so.

The impersonal report. It is believed / said / thought / reported that… and X is believed to have… let a writer pass on a claim without owning it. Broadcast news lives on this structure, and the reading you have just heard uses it in its second sentence.

The two causative patterns with a person. have somebody do something (no to) is close to an instruction; get somebody to do something (with to) suggests persuasion. Neither is the same as have something done, which keeps the worker out of the sentence entirely.

The overlap that catches people. She had the cover made and The cover was made for her describe one event. The first keeps her as the subject and makes the arranging visible; the second puts the object first and lets her disappear. Both are correct; they answer different questions.

The commonest errors at this level
  • Word order in the causative: She had covered the post means she did it, earlier.
  • Participle missing: She had the post cover, It was cover.
  • To after have + person: She had a group to cover it.
  • No to after get + person: She got a group cover it.
  • Adding an agent nobody asked for: It was covered by people.

Two things to watch

1 — The middle slot decides everything. had the post covered against had covered the post: same four words, two different people holding the wool.

2 — Do not stack them. The post was had covered is not a sentence. Choose one shape per clause; if you need both ideas, use two clauses: The post was covered overnight, after she had arranged it with a knitting group.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Choosing the shape that answers the question

The facts: a knitting group covered the lamp posts; the shopkeeper asked them to and paid for the wool.

Step 1 — ask what the sentence is about. If the paragraph is about the street, the street goes first: The lamp posts were covered overnight.

Step 2 — ask whether the worker is news. If the group matters, keep it: …were covered by a local knitting group. If not, drop it.

Step 3 — ask whether the arranging is the story. If it is, the shopkeeper becomes the subject and the causative does the rest: The shopkeeper had the lamp posts covered.

Step 4 — ask whether persuasion is the story. If she had to convince them, name them: She got a local knitting group to cover the lamp posts.

None of these is more correct than the others. Each one answers a different question, and choosing badly is the mistake, not choosing the passive.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Four ways of handling the doer

Active: the doer is the subject — She covered the post. Passive: the doer disappears — The post was covered. Add by only when the doer is the information: It was covered by a local group. Causative: the subject arranged it and somebody else did it — She had the post covered, or informally She got the post covered. Impersonal report: the claim belongs to nobody in particular — It is believed that it started there or It is believed to have started there.

These are not stylistic variants of one sentence; they answer different questions. The post was covered answers what happened to the post?; She had the post covered answers what did she do?; and It is believed to have started there answers neither — it reports a claim while declining to stand behind it.

The impersonal report, and the trap in the middle

Two shapes, same meaning. It + passive + that-clause: It is said that the practice began in Prague. Subject + passive + to-infinitive: The practice is said to have begun in Prague. Use to have + participle when the event is earlier than the reporting, and a plain infinitive when it is not: He is thought to be in his eighties. The verbs that take this pattern are the reporting ones: say, believe, think, know, report, expect, allege, understand.

The trap is the middle pair. She had the post covered means she arranged it; She had covered the post means she had done it herself, earlier. Word order is the only difference, and it changes who did the work. Add the unwelcome reading — He had his window broken — and the same three words cover three quite different situations. Context decides, and at B2 you are expected to read it.

Errors to watch: It is believed that started there → It is believed that it started there · The practice is said to began → to have begun · She had covered the post by a group → had the post covered by a group.

A letter to the council

Somebody has covered the benches outside your building in knitted wool. The council intends to remove it on Friday.

The brief

Write to the council either defending the wool or asking for it to be removed. Whichever side you take, describe what was done and what should be done next without pretending you know who did it. Give one piece of advice, and say what you would have done in the council’s place.

Useful language

1 · Read the model letter.
Model · a letter to the council

Dear Sir or Madam,

Some time on the night of 3 March, the four benches outside Elm House were covered in knitted wool. It is believed to have been done by a group from the community centre, although nobody has claimed it, and I am not in a position to name anybody. I understand that the covers are to be removed on Friday.

I would ask you to reconsider, for two reasons. The first is practical: the wool protects the metal from road salt, and the benches were repainted at some expense two winters ago. The second is that the covers can be removed in ten minutes by one person, which is not true of the graffiti that was there before and which took a contractor most of a day to deal with.

I accept that a precedent is being set, and that it is not the council’s fault that the work was done without permission. My advice would be to leave the covers until the end of April and then have them taken down and stored, rather than destroyed.

If the decision goes the other way, I would advise you to say so publicly, so that the next street does not make the same mistake.

Yours faithfully,
R. Aliyev
